cues.text: Let's start with relational algebra.
This is the formal set of operations that describes how we can work with relations, which are tables, in the relational model.
Think of it as the mathematical toolkit sitting underneath the queries you write in SQL.
The source names six operations.
Let's take them in order.
First, selection.
Selection filters rows.
You give it a condition, and it keeps only the rows that satisfy that condition.
So if you have a table of students and you want only those in a particular department, selection is the operation that does it.
Notice that selection works on rows, and it leaves the columns untouched.
Second, projection.
Projection chooses attributes.
An attribute is simply a column.
Where selection picks rows, projection picks columns.
If you want just the names and matriculation numbers from a student table, you project those two attributes.
Third, union.
Union combines compatible sets.
The word compatible matters here.
For two relations to be combined by union, they must line up in structure, meaning they have the same number of attributes and matching kinds of attributes.
When they do, union gives you one relation containing the rows from both.
Fourth, difference.
Difference removes matching rows.
You start with one relation and take away any rows that also appear in the other.
What remains is what was in the first but not in the second.
Fifth, Cartesian product.
Cartesian product pairs rows.
Every row from the first relation is paired with every row from the second.
So if one table has three rows and another has four, the product has twelve rows.
It pairs everything, whether or not the rows are related, which is why it is rarely useful on its own.
Sixth, join.
Join combines related rows.

This is the practical answer to the limits of the Cartesian product: instead of pairing everything with everything, a join pairs only those rows that are related, typically because they share matching values in a connecting attribute.
Now, a point about how SQL treats all this.
SQL typically preserves duplicates unless DISTINCT is requested.
That is a real difference from the pure mathematical idea of a set, where duplicates cannot exist.
In SQL, if two rows in your result come out identical, both are kept by default.
If you want duplicates removed, you must say so by writing DISTINCT in your query.
Finally, two kinds of join in SQL, and the distinction between them is important.
INNER JOIN returns matches.
Only rows that find a partner on the other side appear in the result.
LEFT JOIN is different: it preserves left rows even without a match.
Every row from the left table appears in the result, and where there is no matching row on the right, the right-side columns are simply left empty.
So the key contrast is this: INNER JOIN drops unmatched rows, while LEFT JOIN keeps all the rows from the left table regardless.
